t: Composed near the end of Hammurabi's reign, the text sets about 4,130 lines of cuneiform on a basalt stele: a poetic prologue and epilogue around laws phrased as “if ... then” cases on criminal, family, property and commercial matters.
Its laws rest on principles such as lex talionis, “an eye for an eye”, and treat people unequally by class and gender, distinguishing the awīlum, the muškēnum and the slave.
Taken as plunder to Susa and found there in 1901, the stele is in the Louvre; scholars still debate whether the text was enforced legislation, a record of past cases or a work of scholarship.
dyk: The epilogue hopes that “any wronged man who has a lawsuit” may have the laws of the stele read aloud to him and know his rights; its curses on any future defacer run to 281 lines.
ev: Hammurabi inherits the throne of Babylon from his father Sin-Muballit, beginning a reign that lasts until around 1750 BCE
The Code is composed near the end of Hammurabi's reign, as the list of his achievements in its prologue shows
The Code appears in a late Babylonian list of literary and scholarly texts, long a part of the scribal curriculum
The French Archaeological Mission under Jacques de Morgan finds the stele in three large fragments on the acropolis of Susa
Jean-Vincent Scheil publishes the editio princeps, with a transliteration and a free translation into French
The codes of Lipit-Ishtar and Ur-Nammu and the Laws of Eshnunna are rediscovered, showing that older law collections existed
Benno Landsberger begins the line of criticism that most judges paid the Code no attention, against the view that it was enforced law

f.made: Hammurabi, sixth king of the Amorite First Dynasty of Babylon, in whose name the text was purportedly written near the end of his reign; the scribes and the draughtsman of the relief, working in a tradition of earlier Sumerian and Akkadian law collections issued by rulers.
f.form: About 4,130 lines of cuneiform in the Old Babylonian dialect of Akkadian: a 300-line prologue and a 500-line epilogue in poetic style around casuistic “if ... then” laws; the primary copy is a basalt stele 2.25 m tall, topped by a relief of Hammurabi with the god Shamash.
f.where: The stele is on the second floor of the Louvre, in Room 227 of the Richelieu wing; over 50 manuscripts of the laws come from Susa, Babylon, Nineveh, Assur, Borsippa, Nippur, Sippar, Ur, Larsa and other sites; replicas stand at the United Nations in New York, the Peace Palace in The Hague and the Pergamon Museum in Berlin.
f.known: lex talionis, “an eye for an eye”; Hammurabi's aim “to prevent the strong from oppressing the weak”; penalties that differ by class and gender; laws on physicians, builders and prices; the curses of the epilogue; the debate over whether it is a true code; comparison with the Covenant Code of Exodus
